name: Celtic
line: Bless the first act of the day, learn a poem by heart, know the story of your place and gather in the evening.

quote.text: People live in each other’s shelter.
quote.source: Ar scáth a chéile a mhaireann na daoine

quotes.text: There is no strength without unity.
quotes.source: Ní neart go cur le chéile

quotes.text: A nation without a language is a nation without a heart.
quotes.source: Cenedl heb iaith, cenedl heb galon

quotes.text: Better broken Gaelic than Gaelic in the coffin.
quotes.source: Is fheàrr Gàidhlig bhriste na Gàidhlig sa chiste

quotes.text: Three candles that illumine every darkness: truth, nature, knowledge.
quotes.source: A collection of about the ninth century, translated by Kuno Meyer, 1906

quotes.text: I am the wind on the sea.
quotes.source: Am gaeth i m-muir. The first line of the poem said to have been spoken by the poet Amergin as he set foot in Ireland; from the Book of Invasions, compiled in the eleventh century

words.usage: The traditional greeting to a guest. Hospitality was a duty in early Irish law, and to refuse it brought dishonour.
The reply goes one better: Dia is Muire dhuit, God and Mary be with you.
Literally, may good be with you.
Said when raising a glass. Slàinte mhath in Scottish Gaelic and iechyd da in Welsh say the same.
Fun, news and banter. What was the craic asks how an evening went.

words.meaning: A visit; a gathering with music and dance
words.usage: Once simply an evening call on neighbours, with stories and songs by the fire. Cèilidh in Scottish Gaelic.
A storyteller who carries the history, genealogy and tales of a district in memory.
Households join to bring in each other’s hay or turf in turn. No money changes hands.
In the early Irish church, the person to whom you opened your whole heart. A saying held that anyone without one is a body without a head.

words.meaning: Heritage; native place; what is in the blood
words.usage: The tie between a person, their people and the land they come from.
The body of stories that explain how each hill, ford and plain got its name. A poet was expected to know them all.
Early Ireland had about a hundred and fifty, each with its own king, assembly and poets.
A member of the learned class, trained for up to twelve years, whose praise made a king’s name and whose satire could ruin it.
A personal taboo laid on a hero. To break it brings ruin, and the old tales turn on the moment it is broken.
The poet’s gift of seeing. It was sought by hazelnuts of wisdom, by sleep and by darkness.
The breath that makes a poet. The bards said it came from the cauldron of the goddess Ceridwen.
Homesickness mixed with grief for a place or time that may no longer exist.
The lift that carries a preacher, a singer or a crowd. Also an everyday goodbye.
First the patch of hill a flock knows as its own, then the surroundings in which a person feels at home.

words.meaning: A hug; a safe small place
words.usage: Both the embrace and the cupboard under the stairs.
Thank you is diolch.

words.meaning: A sitting; a festival of poetry and music
words.usage: A competitive gathering of poets and musicians, first recorded at Cardigan in 1176. The winning poet is seated in a carved chair.

words.meaning: One of the learned priestly class
words.usage: Judges, teachers and keepers of ritual among the ancient Celts. The name probably means oak-knower.
The Greek writers listed three learned orders among the Gauls: bards, seers and druids.
A clearing or wood set apart for the gods. The word survives in place names from Spain to Turkey.
Groups of strokes cut along the edge of a standing stone, used from about the fourth century for names of the dead.

words.meaning: The festival at the start of winter
words.usage: The night of 31 October, when the old year ended and the boundary with the otherworld was thin. The origin of Halloween.

words.meaning: The festival at the start of spring
words.usage: The first of February, the time of the first milk of the ewes and the feast of Saint Brigid.

words.meaning: The festival at the start of summer
words.usage: The first of May. Cattle were driven between two fires before going to the summer pastures.

words.meaning: The festival at the start of harvest
words.usage: The first of August, with assemblies on hilltops, games and the first of the new crop.

practices.name: Bless the first act of the day
practices.instructions: Take the first plain thing you do each morning: lighting the stove, filling the kettle, opening the curtains, washing your face. Before you do it, stop. Say a few words over it aloud, in your own language and your own belief or none: may this fire warm the house, may this water wash me clean. Then do it. The rule of this Onda is to bless the ordinary.
practices.why: The Carmina Gadelica, collected in the Scottish Highlands and islands in the 19th century, is full of blessings for kindling the fire, milking the cow and washing the face. They make everyday tasks into small ceremonies.
variations: Write your own blessing for the kettle.
Say it in Irish, Welsh or Gaelic if you can.

practices.name: Learn a poem by heart
practices.instructions: Choose a poem or a song that you love and learn four lines of it today. Say them aloud ten times, walking if you can. Cover the page and say them again. Add four more lines tomorrow. By the end of the month you will carry a whole poem in your head. The rule of this Onda is to carry it in your head.
practices.why: Poets in the Celtic lands, the filí and the bards, trained for years to hold thousands of lines in memory. A poem learned by heart goes with you everywhere.
variations: Choose a poem in a Celtic language.

practices.name: A bowl of porridge
practices.instructions: Make porridge with oatmeal and water or milk, stirring clockwise with a spoon and adding a pinch of salt. Cook it slowly until thick. Eat it standing, if you like, in the Scots way, with cream or a little honey, as a bowl of old Celtic comfort. Oats were the staple of the Highlands. Say a word of thanks as you start.
practices.why: Porridge is the traditional breakfast of Scotland and the oat-growing parts of Ireland and Wales. A bowl is simple, warm and strengthening.
variations: Add a pinch of salt not sugar.

practices.name: Turn sunwise
practices.instructions: Walk once around your house, garden, or a tree, in the direction of the sun, clockwise, as a morning blessing. This is the deiseal, the sunwise turn, which Celtic tradition held to bring good luck. Say a short wish as you go: peace on this house and all in it. Keep it simple and quiet.
practices.why: Deiseal, turning with the sun, was done to bring blessing, from rounds of the house to circling a well. It is a small action that carries a feeling of order.

practices.name: Greet in a Celtic language
practices.instructions: Greet three people today in a Celtic language: dia dhuit in Irish, bore da in Welsh, madainn mhath in Scottish Gaelic, demat in Breton. Say thank you too: go raibh maith agat, diolch, tapadh leat, trugarez. Learn the pronunciation online first. Use the greeting with a smile.
practices.why: The Celtic languages, Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Manx, Welsh, Cornish and Breton, are alive and being revived. Learning a greeting is a friendly gesture.

practices.name: Wait for the awen
practices.instructions: Sit quietly with a pen and paper for ten minutes and wait for awen, the Welsh word for poetic inspiration, flowing spirit. Do not force anything. Write whatever arrives: a line, an image, a name. If nothing comes, write that. The bards held that awen came to the prepared. Read what you wrote aloud.
practices.why: Awen is the Welsh bardic idea of inspiration, which was said to flow from the cauldron of the goddess Ceridwen. A short quiet writing is a simple way to invite it.

practices.name: Learn the lore of one place
practices.instructions: Pick one place within walking distance: a hill, a street, a stream, a field, a crossroads, a well. Find out what its name means and what happened there. Ask an older neighbour, read the map, look in a local history. Then go and stand in it for ten minutes. In Ireland this lore is dinnseanchas, the lore of places. The rule of this Onda is to know your place.
practices.why: Dinnseanchas, the lore of places, was a branch of learning for the Irish poets. Every field and hill had a story attached to its name.
variations: Look up the name in a place-name dictionary.
Ask a neighbour what they know.
Write the story on a card.

practices.name: Weave a Brigid’s cross
practices.instructions: Weave a Brigid’s cross from rushes, straw or strips of paper: fold a rush around the centre of another at right angles, turn it a quarter and fold the next one around, and repeat until you have a square cross with four arms. Tie the ends. St Brigid’s Day, on 1 February, is when crosses are made in Ireland. Hang it over your door.
practices.why: The Brigid’s cross is woven on the eve of 1 February, and hung over the door for protection through the year. Making one takes half an hour.
variations: Make several and give them away.
Learn the pattern from a video.

practices.name: Bake soda bread
practices.instructions: Bake soda bread: mix flour, a teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda, a pinch of salt and enough buttermilk to make a soft dough. Shape into a round, cut a deep cross on top and bake until golden and hollow-sounding when tapped. The cross was said to let the fairies out. Eat it warm with butter.
practices.why: Soda bread is the everyday bread of Ireland, quick to make without yeast. A fresh loaf warms the house.
variations: Share a loaf with a neighbour.

practices.name: Meitheal
practices.instructions: Take part in a meitheal, an Irish work party: help a neighbour with a job, or ask neighbours to help with yours. Harvest, move stones, clear a path, bring in the turf, mend a wall. Work alongside each other, talk and sing. The one helped provides the tea and the food. The rule of this Onda is to keep an open door.
practices.why: The meitheal was a cooperative work group of neighbours, who helped each other with big jobs in rural Ireland. The tradition lives on.
variations: Offer a neighbour a morning’s help.

practices.name: A game of brandub
practices.instructions: Play brandub, the Irish board game of the early Middle Ages. Draw a grid of 7 by 7 squares. One player has a king and four defenders in the centre; the other has eight attackers at the edges. The king wins by reaching a corner; the attackers by capturing him. Play two games with a friend.
practices.why: Brandub, black raven, was played in Ireland by the 6th century and mentioned in the old tales. It is simple, tense and quick.
variations: Draw the board on a piece of cloth.

practices.name: Go to the water
practices.instructions: Walk to a spring, a stream, a fountain or the sea and stand beside it for ten minutes. In Celtic lands holy wells were visited on saints’ days, with prayers, rags tied to a nearby tree and a drink of water. You need not believe in anything; just notice the water, how it moves, and where it comes from. Leave a small clean stone beside it.
practices.why: Holy wells are all over the Celtic countries, places where water meets belief. Visiting one is a quiet pleasure.
variations: Find the nearest well on a map.
Pour a little water on a plant.

practices.name: Make a triad
practices.instructions: Look back on the day and sum up something you learned in a group of three. Three things that are better shared. Three signs of a good neighbour. Three things I will not do again. Write it in one line, in the old form: three things... The Welsh Triads and the Irish triads were memory aids for wisdom and lore.
practices.why: The triad is a Celtic form of wise saying, such as the Trioedd Ynys Prydain, the Welsh Triads. Making one each evening is a short, thoughtful habit.
variations: Write a triad about the weather.

practices.name: Go visiting, or be visited
practices.instructions: Spend the evening in company with no screen. Call on a neighbour or ask people in. When you are settled, go round the room, and let everyone give one thing: a song, a tune, a poem, a story, a joke, a riddle, a piece of news. Nobody is forced; everyone is invited. The Irish word is céilí, a visit. The rule of this Onda is to bring your piece.
practices.why: The céilí house, where neighbours gathered nightly to tell stories, sing and dance, was the heart of Celtic rural life. Anyone could come and everyone was expected to give something.
variations: Take a bottle of juice and a poem.
Ask each guest for a story.

practices.name: A seanchaí’s tale
practices.instructions: Tell a folktale as a seanchaí, an Irish storyteller, would: sit by a lamp or a fire and begin with a formula, such as once upon a time, long ago. Choose a tale of Fionn, Cú Chulainn or a Welsh story from the Mabinogion, such as the birth of Taliesin. Tell it in your own words, slowly. Let the listeners ask what happened next.
practices.why: The seanchaí was the keeper of tales in the Irish and Scottish Gaelic communities, who could tell stories for hours. Telling one is a gift.
variations: Tell it in two sentences, then in ten.

practices.name: Smoor the fire
practices.instructions: Close the day as the Gaelic households did when they smoored the fire: cover the embers with ash and peat, make the sign of the cross or a circle over them and say a blessing for the house through the night. At home, put out a candle or switch off the last light with a blessing. Say: peace to this house and all in it till morning. Never leave a flame unattended.
practices.why: The Carmina Gadelica gives several prayers for smooring the fire at night, to keep the household safe. A modern version is a short blessing at lights-out.
variations: Say it aloud in the dark.
Bless each room as you go.

practices.name: Listen to the harp
practices.instructions: Play a recording of the Celtic harp, such as Alan Stivell’s Renaissance de la harpe celtique, or the music of Turlough O’Carolan, the blind Irish harper. Sit still and listen, with a cup of tea. Close your eyes. The harp was the instrument of the Celtic kings, and the bards sang to its strings.
practices.why: The harp is the national emblem of Ireland, and Brittany’s Alan Stivell revived the Celtic harp in the 1970s. Its sound is gentle and luminous.
variations: Listen to Julie Fowlis in Gaelic.

practices.name: A note on hiraeth
practices.instructions: Write a short note about a place or a time that you miss, in the manner of hiraeth, the Welsh word for longing for a home that no longer exists or never was. Describe it in a few lines with a few details: the smell, the sound, the light. Then say what you can do today to carry some of it forward.
practices.why: Hiraeth is a Welsh word with no exact English equivalent, a mixture of homesickness, grief and longing. Writing about it is a way of honouring a place.
variations: Write to someone who shares the memory.

practices.name: A ceilidh
practices.instructions: Hold a ceilidh, a party with dancing, in a hall or a big room. Invite friends of all ages, ask someone to call the dances, and put on a fiddle and accordion record. Dance simple group dances: the Gay Gordons, the Dashing White Sergeant or a céilí set. Take turns singing a song or telling a joke between dances. Serve tea and sandwiches.
practices.why: The ceilidh is a social gathering with dancing, singing and storytelling, popular across Ireland and Scotland. Anyone can join and everyone can be taught a step.
variations: Learn the Gay Gordons from a video.

practices.name: Climb a hill with a story
practices.instructions: Choose a hill near you, find a story about it, and climb it with a friend. Tell the story at the top, and look around at the view. In the Celtic lands hills are sacred places with stories: Tara, Croagh Patrick, Tryfan, Ben Lomond. Dress for the weather, take water and tell someone where you are going. Leave nothing behind.
practices.why: Celtic peoples loved hills and mountains and made them places of assembly and story. A walk with a tale makes any hill special.
variations: Look up the name of the hill.
Take a notebook for the view.

immersePlan.name: Read a branch of the Mabinogion
immersePlan.text: Read one of the Four Branches, perhaps Pwyll and Rhiannon. Sioned Davies’s translation keeps the oral voice. Retell it in your own words.

immersePlan.name: Read from Carmina Gadelica
immersePlan.text: Read a few blessings from the great collection of Highland prayers and charms. Choose one for your own door.

immersePlan.name: Read from The Islandman
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Tomás Ó Criomhthain’s memoir of life on the Great Blasket Island, a classic of Irish writing. Note the details of daily work.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Secret of Kells
immersePlan.text: Watch Tomm Moore’s 2009 animated film about a boy who helps to make the Book of Kells. Watch the patterns.

immersePlan.name: Watch Song of the Sea
immersePlan.text: Watch Tomm Moore’s 2014 animated film of a boy and his selkie sister on the Irish coast. It is gentle and magical.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Quiet Girl
immersePlan.text: Watch Colm Bairéad’s 2022 film in Irish about a withdrawn girl sent to spend a summer with relatives in rural Ireland. Quiet and moving.

immersePlan.name: Listen to The Chieftains
immersePlan.text: Play the 1973 album by Ireland’s best-known traditional band, with pipes, fiddle and harp. Tap your foot.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Julie Fowlis
immersePlan.text: Play Julie Fowlis’s 2007 album of Scottish Gaelic songs, with a clear voice and delicate arrangements.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Joe Heaney
immersePlan.text: Play the great sean-nós singer of Connemara in recordings from the 1960s. Listen to the long, ornamented lines. This artist has passed away.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Book of Kells
immersePlan.text: Look at pages of the great illuminated Gospel book made about 800. Pick a page and trace one of the knots with your eyes.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Tara Brooch
immersePlan.text: Look at the Irish gold and silver brooch of about 700, decorated with filigree and amber. Count the animal heads.

immersePlan.name: Look at Muiredach’s Cross
immersePlan.text: Look at the tall carved stone cross at Monasterboice, with Bible scenes in relief. Find a scene you recognise.

immersePlan.name: Bake soda bread
immersePlan.text: Mix flour, soda, salt and buttermilk into a dough, cut a cross and bake until golden. Eat warm with butter.

immersePlan.name: Make colcannon
immersePlan.text: Mash potatoes with kale or cabbage, spring onions, butter and cream. It is the dish of Halloween in Ireland.

immersePlan.name: Bake oatcakes
immersePlan.text: Mix oatmeal, water and a little fat into a stiff dough and bake thin rounds on a griddle. Eat with cheese.

immersePlan.name: Learn about uisce beatha
immersePlan.text: Whiskey is uisce beatha, the water of life, in Irish and Gaelic. Read about it, and drink a hot cup of water with honey, lemon and a clove instead.

immersePlan.name: Drink apple juice from a bowl
immersePlan.text: In Brittany cider is drunk from a pottery bowl. Pour cloudy apple juice into a bowl and sip it with a buckwheat galette.

immersePlan.name: Brew a strong pot of tea
immersePlan.text: Brew a strong pot of tea and drink it with milk. In Ireland tea is the drink of welcome.

immersePlan.name: Make a Brigid’s cross
immersePlan.text: Weave a four-armed cross from rushes or paper and hang it over your door.

immersePlan.name: Turn sunwise
immersePlan.text: Walk once around a tree or your house clockwise, with a short wish.

immersePlan.name: Visit a well or spring
immersePlan.text: Visit a spring, a fountain or a stream and spend ten minutes beside it. Leave a small stone.

immersePlan.name: Learn about hurling
immersePlan.text: Watch a clip of hurling, one of the oldest and fastest field games in the world, played with a stick and a small ball. Throw a ball into the air and catch it.

immersePlan.name: Play brandub
immersePlan.text: Play the early Irish board game on a 7 by 7 grid with coins and pebbles.

immersePlan.name: Learn about shinty
immersePlan.text: Watch a clip of the Highland game of shinty, a cousin of hurling played with a curved stick. Notice the speed.

immersePlan.name: Mark Samhain
immersePlan.text: Samhain, 31 October to 1 November, marks the end of the harvest and the start of winter. Light a candle, remember someone who has died and eat colcannon.

immersePlan.name: Mark Imbolc
immersePlan.text: Imbolc, 1 February, marks the first stirrings of spring and the feast of St Brigid. Make a cross and light a candle.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Eisteddfod
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the great Welsh festival of poetry and music, held every August. Read a winning poem in translation.

immersePlan.name: Say céad míle fáilte
immersePlan.text: Céad míle fáilte means a hundred thousand welcomes. Say it to every guest today.

immersePlan.name: Think about hiraeth
immersePlan.text: Hiraeth is a Welsh longing for home. Name a place you miss and what you loved there.

immersePlan.name: Practise craic
immersePlan.text: Craic is good fun and talk. Spend half an hour in lively, easy company.

rules.why: Welcome the guest and feed them before you ask their business.
Learn poems, songs and stories by heart. What is in memory cannot be taken.
Learn the names and the stories of the land you live on.
Mark the small acts of the day with a word of thanks.
Have a song or a story ready, and give it when asked.
Speak it, however badly. Better broken than in the coffin.

read.title: The Táin
read.creator: Translated by Thomas Kinsella
read.why: The cattle raid of Cooley. Queen Medb’s army invades Ulster to steal a bull and the boy hero Cú Chulainn holds the ford alone. The great epic of early Ireland.

read.title: The Mabinogion
read.creator: Translated by Sioned Davies
read.why: Eleven medieval Welsh tales of shape-shifting, otherworld kings and the earliest Arthur, in a translation made to be read aloud.

read.title: Carmina Gadelica
read.creator: Collected by Alexander Carmichael
read.why: Hymns, charms and blessings taken down from Gaelic speakers in the Hebrides: prayers for the fire, the cow, the loom and the road.

read.title: The Islandman
read.creator: Tomás Ó Criomhthain
read.why: A fisherman of the Great Blasket Island sets down his life in Irish, so that there would be a record, as he wrote, for the like of us will never be again.

read.title: The Celts: A Very Short Introduction
read.creator: Barry Cunliffe
read.why: A clear account of who the Celts were, and of how the idea of them has been made and remade.

read.title: Anam Cara
read.creator: John O’Donohue
read.why: A poet and former priest from the west of Ireland on friendship, solitude and belonging.

watch.title: The Secret of Kells
watch.creator: Tomm Moore and Nora Twomey
watch.why: A boy in a monastery under threat from the Vikings helps to finish a great book. Drawn in the patterns of the manuscript itself.

watch.title: Song of the Sea
watch.creator: Tomm Moore
watch.why: A lighthouse keeper’s daughter turns out to be a selkie, a seal who can take human form. Animated in Kilkenny, with songs in Irish.

watch.title: The Quiet Girl
watch.creator: Colm Bairéad
watch.why: An Cailín Ciúin. A neglected child spends a summer with relatives on a farm. A film in Irish of great tenderness and few words.

watch.title: Hedd Wyn
watch.creator: Paul Turner
watch.why: A Welsh shepherd poet wins the chair at the National Eisteddfod of 1917, six weeks after his death in the trenches. In Welsh.

listen.title: The Chieftains 4
listen.creator: The Chieftains
listen.why: Pipes, fiddles, whistle, harp and bodhrán playing the old dance tunes and slow airs.

listen.title: Renaissance de la harpe celtique
listen.creator: Alan Stivell
listen.why: A Breton musician and the wire-strung harp his father rebuilt. The record that began the Celtic music revival.

listen.title: Cuilidh
listen.creator: Julie Fowlis
listen.why: Songs in Scottish Gaelic from North Uist, among them the quick mouth music sung for dancing.

listen.title: The Road from Connemara
listen.creator: Joe Heaney
listen.why: A master of sean-nós, the old unaccompanied style of singing in Irish, with his stories of the songs.

listen.title: Yma o Hyd
listen.creator: Dafydd Iwan
listen.why: Still here. A Welsh song of survival against the odds that became an anthem of the language and of the national football team.

art.title: The Book of Kells
art.creator: Monks of Iona and Kells
art.why: The four Gospels in Latin, with pages of interlace, spirals and animals so fine that a medieval visitor took it for the work of angels. In Trinity College, Dublin.

art.title: The Battersea Shield
art.creator: A British metalworker
art.why: A bronze shield facing with flowing raised curves and red glass, found in the River Thames, where it was probably cast as an offering. In the British Museum.

art.title: The Tara Brooch
art.creator: An Irish goldsmith
art.why: A cloak pin in gilded silver, amber and glass, with decoration on the back as fine as on the front. In the National Museum of Ireland.

art.title: Muiredach’s Cross
art.creator: The carvers of Monasterboice
art.why: A ringed stone cross five and a half metres tall, covered with scenes from the Bible. It stands where it was raised, in County Louth.

eat.title: Soda bread
eat.creator: Flour, buttermilk, salt and soda
eat.why: Mixed in minutes and baked in a pot over the fire. A cross is cut in the top.

eat.title: Colcannon
eat.creator: Mashed potato with kale or cabbage and butter
eat.why: The dish of Halloween night, with a ring or a coin hidden in it to tell fortunes.

eat.title: Cawl
eat.creator: A Welsh broth of lamb, leeks and roots
eat.why: Kept going for days and better on the second. Eaten with bread and cheese.

eat.title: Buckwheat galette
eat.creator: A thin dark pancake from Brittany
eat.why: Filled with egg, ham and cheese and folded into a square.

eat.title: Oatcakes
eat.creator: Oatmeal, water and a little fat
eat.why: The bread of the Scottish Highlands, baked on a griddle.

drink.title: Whiskey
drink.creator: The water of life
drink.why: The word comes from the Gaelic uisce beatha. Distilled by Irish and Scottish monks from at least the fifteenth century.

drink.title: Breton cider
drink.creator: Drunk from a pottery bowl
drink.why: The drink that goes with galettes.

drink.title: Strong tea
drink.creator: With milk
drink.why: The first thing offered to anyone who comes through the door in Ireland.

customs.title: Brigid’s cross
customs.creator: Woven on the eve of 1 February
customs.why: A cross of four arms plaited from green rushes and hung over the door to protect the house for the year.

customs.title: Turning sunwise
customs.creator: Deiseal, with the sun
customs.why: One walks round a well, a church or a fishing boat in the direction the sun travels. The other way is unlucky.

customs.title: The wake
customs.creator: Sitting up with the dead
customs.why: Neighbours keep the family company through the night with tea, drink, talk and stories about the one who has died.

customs.title: Holy wells
customs.creator: Visited on a saint’s day
customs.why: Pilgrims circle the well, drink and tie a strip of cloth to the tree beside it.

games.title: Hurling
games.creator: Field game · Ireland
games.year: at least two thousand years old
games.why: Fifteen a side strike a small ball with ash sticks at great speed. Cú Chulainn plays it in the sagas. The women’s game is camogie.

games.title: Shinty
games.creator: Field game · Scottish Highlands
games.why: Camanachd, a cousin of hurling brought from Ireland with the Gaelic language.

games.title: Brandub
games.creator: Board game · Ireland
games.why: A king and four defenders at the centre of a seven by seven board try to reach a corner past eight attackers.

games.title: Gouren
games.creator: Wrestling · Brittany
games.why: Wrestlers in loose linen shirts swear an oath of fair play and try to throw each other flat on the back. Cornwall has a sister style.

games.title: Highland games
games.creator: Athletics · Scotland
games.why: Tossing the caber, putting the stone and throwing the hammer, with piping and dancing.

festivals.title: Samhain
festivals.creator: 31 October to 1 November
festivals.why: The start of winter and of the Celtic year. Fires were lit, the dead were remembered and people went out in disguise.

festivals.title: Imbolc
festivals.creator: 1 February
festivals.why: Saint Brigid’s Day, the first stirring of spring. A public holiday in Ireland since 2023.

festivals.title: Bealtaine
festivals.creator: 1 May
festivals.why: The start of summer. Bonfires are lit again each year on the Hill of Uisneach and on Calton Hill in Edinburgh.

festivals.title: Lughnasa
festivals.creator: 1 August
festivals.why: The start of harvest. Its descendants include the climb of Croagh Patrick on the last Sunday of July.

festivals.title: The National Eisteddfod of Wales
festivals.creator: The first week of August
festivals.why: Eight days of competition in poetry, song and recitation, held entirely in Welsh at a different place each year.

festivals.title: Festival Interceltique
festivals.creator: Early August, Lorient, Brittany
festivals.why: Musicians and pipe bands from all the Celtic countries, with hundreds of thousands of visitors.

places.title: The Hill of Tara
places.creator: County Meath, Ireland
places.why: A low green ridge of earthworks, the seat of the high kings in tradition, with the standing stone said to cry out under a true king.

places.title: Skellig Michael
places.creator: Off County Kerry, Ireland
places.why: A rock in the Atlantic with a monastery of stone beehive cells near its summit, reached by six hundred steps cut by the monks.

places.title: Iona
places.creator: Inner Hebrides, Scotland
places.why: The small island where Columba founded his monastery in 563. The Book of Kells was probably begun here.

places.title: Dún Aonghasa
places.creator: Inis Mór, Aran Islands, Ireland
places.why: A great stone fort of three ramparts on the edge of a hundred-metre cliff, first built about three thousand years ago.

places.title: Hallstatt
places.creator: Upper Austria
places.why: The lakeside salt-mining village whose rich graves gave their name to the earliest Celtic culture.

places.title: The Laténium
places.creator: Neuchâtel, Switzerland
places.why: The museum beside the lake where thousands of swords, brooches and shields were found in 1857, giving the La Tène style its name.

ethics.title: Hospitality
ethics.text: The guest is welcomed and fed without question.
ethics.practice: Offer food or drink to whoever comes to your door.

ethics.title: Honour
ethics.text: A person is their good name.
ethics.practice: Keep one promise today that it would be easier to break.

ethics.title: Truth in speech
ethics.text: A just word upholds the land. A false judgment blights it.
ethics.practice: Say what is true where it costs you something.

ethics.title: Generosity
ethics.text: A leader is measured by open-handedness.

ethics.title: Loyalty to kin and place
ethics.text: You belong to a people and a piece of land.
ethics.practice: Do something for the place you come from.

ethics.title: Courage
ethics.text: The sagas honour those who stand at the ford.
ethics.practice: Hold your ground on one thing today.

philosophy.title: The spoken word
philosophy.text: The druids chose not to write their teaching down. Knowledge lived in trained memory.
philosophy.practice: What do you know that you could recite without help?

philosophy.title: The power of the poet
philosophy.text: A poet’s praise made a reputation and a satire could raise blisters on a king’s face.
philosophy.practice: What can words do that force cannot?

philosophy.title: The otherworld beside us
philosophy.text: The other realm is not far off. It lies under the hills and across the water and may be stepped into at certain times and places.
philosophy.practice: Where does the ordinary world feel thin to you?

philosophy.title: Threes
philosophy.text: Wisdom was shaped in triads so that it could be held and handed on.
philosophy.practice: What three things do you know to be true?

philosophy.title: The prince’s truth
philosophy.text: Early Irish texts say that the ruler’s justice brings good weather, full nets and peace, and his falsehood brings famine.
philosophy.practice: What depends on your being fair?

philosophy.title: Place and name
philosophy.text: A place is its stories. To lose the names is to lose the country.
philosophy.practice: What stories does your home ground hold?

philosophy.title: Longing
philosophy.text: Hiraeth is counted a kind of love and not an illness.
philosophy.practice: What do you long for that cannot be had back?

philosophy.title: A small language
philosophy.text: Each of the Celtic languages has been close to death and each has people who refuse to let it go.
philosophy.practice: What would you keep alive against the odds?

intro: The word Celtic has two meanings, and it helps to keep them apart. The first is ancient. Greek and Roman writers used Celts, Gauls and Galatians for the peoples who lived north of the Alps from about the sixth century BC, across what are now France, southern Germany, Austria, Switzerland, northern Italy and parts of Spain. The second is modern. Since about 1700 it has been the name of a family of languages, and of the peoples who speak them: Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Manx on one branch, Welsh, Breton and Cornish on the other.

The ancient Celts were never one nation. They were hundreds of tribes with related languages, similar gods and a shared style of art. Archaeologists name their earliest culture after Hallstatt in Austria, where salt-mining chieftains were buried with wagons and Greek wine vessels, and its successor, from about 450 BC, after La Tène in Switzerland. La Tène metalwork, with its swirling, never quite symmetrical curves, is among the finest art of ancient Europe. Celtic warriors sacked Rome about 390 BC, raided Delphi in 279 BC and settled in the middle of what is now Turkey. Their learned class, the druids, were priests, judges and teachers who committed nothing to writing.

Between 225 and 50 BC Rome conquered them. Julius Caesar’s war in Gaul ended with the surrender of Vercingetorix in 52 BC, and Britain followed a century later. On the continent the Celtic languages died out under Latin. They survived on the Atlantic edge, in Britain and above all in Ireland, which Rome never reached.

There the old culture met Christianity and produced something new. From the fifth century Irish monasteries became centres of learning. Their monks copied the Gospels in manuscripts such as the Book of Kells, sailed as missionaries to Scotland and the continent, and wrote down the sagas of their own pagan past, which is why we have them. Irish and Welsh kingdoms kept their own law, administered by professional jurists, and their own schools of poetry for a thousand years.

From the twelfth century the Celtic-speaking countries were conquered or absorbed, one after another, by England and France. The languages were shut out of law, school and government. Clearance, famine and emigration emptied the Highlands and the west of Ireland in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and scattered their people across the world. Manx and Cornish ceased to be anyone’s first language.

They have not died. Welsh is spoken by more than half a million people and is the daily language of much of north and west Wales. Irish is the first official language of Ireland. Breton, Gaelic, Manx and Cornish all have schools, broadcasting and new young speakers. The music, the games and the festivals are everywhere.

A warning is needed. Much of what is sold as ancient Celtic wisdom, from tree calendars to druid ceremonies, was invented in the last two hundred and fifty years. This Onda keeps to what is attested: hospitality, memory, place-lore, the triad and the evening gathering.
guide.origin: Ancient central and western Europe, and today Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Brittany, Cornwall and the Isle of Man
guide.era: The Celts enter history about 800 to 500 BC. Some two million people speak a Celtic language today

figures.name: Vercingetorix
figures.bio: A young chief of the Arverni who united the tribes of Gaul against Caesar, was besieged at Alesia, surrendered to save his people and was executed in Rome.

figures.name: Boudica
figures.bio: Queen of the Iceni in eastern Britain. After the Romans flogged her and assaulted her daughters she led a rising that burned three cities.

figures.name: Saint Patrick
figures.bio: A Briton carried to Ireland as a slave at sixteen, who escaped and returned as a missionary. Two short writings of his own survive.

figures.name: Brigid of Kildare
figures.bio: Founder of a great double monastery for women and men. Her legends of generosity, fire and cattle carry echoes of an older goddess of the same name.

figures.name: Columba
figures.bio: Colum Cille, a prince of the northern Uí Néill who left Ireland and founded the monastery of Iona, from which Scotland and northern England were evangelised.

figures.name: Taliesin
figures.bio: A poet at the courts of northern Britain, to whom a few of the oldest poems in Welsh are credited. Later legend made him a shape-shifting seer.

figures.name: Hywel Dda
figures.bio: Hywel the Good, king of most of Wales, under whose name the laws of the country were set in order. They gave women notable rights in property and divorce.

figures.name: Brian Boru
figures.bio: A minor king from Munster who made himself high king of all Ireland and died in his tent after victory at Clontarf.

figures.name: Dafydd ap Gwilym
figures.bio: The greatest of Welsh poets, who wrote of love, birds, mist and his own misadventures in intricate strict metre.

figures.name: Gráinne Mhaol
figures.bio: Grace O’Malley, chieftain and sea captain on the coast of Mayo, who sailed to London in 1593 to negotiate with Elizabeth I in person.

figures.name: Turlough O'Carolan
figures.bio: A blind harper who rode from house to house across Ireland composing tunes for his hosts. More than two hundred survive.

figures.name: Douglas Hyde
figures.bio: A collector of Irish songs and founder of the Gaelic League, which began the revival of the language. He became the first president of Ireland.

history.detail: Iron-using chiefdoms north of the Alps grow rich on salt and on trade with the Greeks and Etruscans.
A new art style and a warrior aristocracy spread from the Marne and the Rhine across Europe.
Gauls from the Po valley defeat a Roman army and hold the city to ransom.
A Celtic host raids Greece. Three tribes cross into Asia Minor and found Galatia.
Rome conquers Gaul in eight campaigns. Caesar’s account is the fullest description of the Celts and their druids.
Rome invades. The druids’ stronghold on Anglesey is destroyed in 60, and Boudica rises the same year.
Ireland becomes Christian. Monasteries are founded at Armagh, Clonmacnoise and Iona, and Britons crossing the sea give Brittany its name and language.
Irish art reaches its height as the first Viking raids begin.
Normans land in Ireland. Edward I of England conquers Wales and kills its last native prince.
Wales is joined to England by law and Welsh is barred from public office. The Gaelic lords of Ulster flee and their lands are settled from Britain.
The Welsh scholar Edward Lhuyd shows that Irish, Gaelic, Welsh, Cornish and Breton are related to one another and to ancient Gaulish, and calls them Celtic.
After Culloden the Highland clans are broken and their people evicted for sheep. In Ireland the potato fails. A million die and more than a million leave.
The Gaelic League is founded. The Irish Free State is established with Irish as its national language.
A radio lecture on the fate of Welsh sets off a campaign of protest. Welsh, Gaelic and Irish gain legal status, television channels and schools.

concepts.detail: No ancient writer called the people of Britain or Ireland Celts. The link is one of language, made by scholars around 1700, and it is real.
Classical authors describe three classes of the wise. In Ireland the poets inherited much of the druids’ standing after Christianity came.
Law, genealogy, history and poetry were carried in verse by trained specialists. Writing arrived with the church.
The Irish sídh mounds, the Welsh Annwn and the western isles of the ever-young are places of feasting without age, entered through hills, lakes and mist.
Samhain, Imbolc, Bealtaine and Lughnasa divided the Irish year into four. The eight-spoked wheel of the year is a twentieth-century addition.
Each free person had an honour price. Refusing food and shelter, or enduring a poet’s satire, could cost it.
Irish Brehon law and the Welsh law of Hywel were kept by a professional class and settled wrongs by compensation.
The Irish church grew around monasteries. Its monks prized exile for the love of God, strict penance and poems in praise of blackbirds and the sea.
From the eighteenth century poets and scholars recovered the old literature and also made things up, including the druid ceremonies of the Welsh Gorsedd, devised in 1792.

facts.text: Halloween, with its disguises and its lanterns, comes from Samhain. The first lanterns were carved from turnips.
A Welsh-speaking community has lived in Patagonia, in Argentina, since 1865.
The Galatians to whom Saint Paul wrote were descendants of Celts who settled in Asia Minor.
Paris takes its name from a Gaulish tribe, the Parisii.
Irish has the oldest written literature in a native language of any people north of the Alps.
The last person to grow up speaking Manx, Ned Maddrell, died in 1974. Children are now taught entirely in Manx at a school on the island.

sensitivity.note: The Celtic languages and their communities are alive, and each of the six nations has its own history. This Onda was written from published sources and keeps to what is attested in old texts and living custom. Speakers of the languages are invited to correct it.
requiredCaveats: Much popular Celtic spirituality is modern. The tree calendar, most druid ritual and the eightfold wheel of the year date from the eighteenth to the twentieth centuries.
Almost everything written about the ancient druids comes from Greek and Roman authors, some of them enemies. Very little is certain.
Whether the peoples of ancient Britain and Ireland should be called Celts at all is debated by scholars. The shared family of languages is not in doubt.
The languages were suppressed for centuries and are still under pressure. Pronunciations given here are rough guides and vary by dialect.
